summary: Describes a simple protocol for delivering real-time events to user agents using HTTP/2 server push. A server can send notifications to a client without waiting for the client to ask each time.

plainLanguage.summary: Web push is how a server reaches a phone that is not busy doing anything else. The phone holds one open connection to a push service, the server sends the event to that service, and the service passes it down the connection. The phone then tells the service it got the message, and the service can tell the server. One connection carries the events for every app on the device, which saves the phone's battery.

questions: how to push real-time events over http
how does http/2 server push deliver events
what is the ttl header in web push
what is a push message urgency
subtitle: A standard way for a server to push events to a phone without the phone keeping a connection open.

tldr.problem: Applications on phones and embedded devices need to receive events such as incoming calls or messages promptly, but the radio is the most expensive part of a device's energy budget. Every application keeping its own open connection adds its own overhead, and the keep-alive traffic needed to stop middleboxes dropping those connections can cost more than the events themselves.
tldr.mechanism: A push service sits between the application server and the device. The device subscribes once, the application server sends messages to the push service, and the push service holds them and delivers them over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection using server push. The RFC defines the resources, the header fields for time-to-live, urgency and topic replacement, and the acknowledgement and receipt flow.
tldr.outcome: One connection serves every application on the device, and messages can be stored while the device is offline and delivered when it returns. The RFC requires TLS and end-to-end message encryption, because the push service sits in the middle and would otherwise be able to read every message.

facts.label: Default port used in the examples

today: RFC 8030 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It uses HTTP/2 server push from RFC 7540 and registers the system port 1001 for the webpush service.

sections.title: Why Push Needs a Standard Protocol
sections.content:
Many applications on mobile and embedded devices need continuous access to network communications so that real-time events, such as incoming calls or messages, can be delivered in a timely fashion. These devices typically have limited power reserves, so finding more efficient ways to serve application requirements greatly benefits the application ecosystem.

One significant contributor to power usage is the radio. Uncoordinated use of persistent connections or sessions from multiple applications can contribute to unnecessary use of the device radio, since each independent session can incur its own overhead. In particular, the keep-alive traffic used to ensure that middleboxes do not prematurely time out sessions can waste a lot of power. Maintenance traffic tends to dominate over the long term, since events are relatively rare.

Consolidating all real-time events into a single session ensures more efficient use of network and radio resources. A single service consolidates all events and distributes them to applications as they arrive, which needs just one session and avoids duplicated overhead costs.

The W3C Push API describes an API that enables the use of a consolidated push service from web applications. This document expands on that work by describing a protocol that can be used to request the delivery of a push message to a user agent, to create new push message delivery subscriptions, and to monitor for new push messages. A standardized method of event delivery is particularly important for the W3C Push API, where application servers might need to use multiple push services. The subscription, management and monitoring functions are currently fulfilled by proprietary protocols, which are adequate but offer none of the advantages that standardization affords. This document intentionally does not describe how a push service is discovered; user agents are expected to be configured with a URL for a push service.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping a phone's connection open to every app is expensive, because the radio has to be woken regularly just to keep the connection alive. One connection carrying every app's events costs far less. Before this RFC there was no standard way to arrange that, so each push service did it its own way.

sections.title: The Three Actors and Their Resources
sections.content:
A general model for push services has three actors: a user agent, a push service, and an application server. At the very beginning a new message subscription is created by the user agent and then distributed to its application server, and that subscription is the basis of all future interactions between the actors. The application server uses the subscription to send messages to the push service for delivery to the user agent, and the user agent uses the subscription to monitor the push service for any incoming message.

To offer more control for authorization, a message subscription is modelled as two resources with different capabilities. A subscription resource is used to receive messages from a subscription and to delete a subscription, and it is private to the user agent. A push resource is used to send messages to a subscription, and it is public and shared by the user agent with its application server. It is expected that a unique subscription will be distributed to each application, but the protocol has no inherent cardinality constraints, and sharing subscriptions has security and privacy implications. Subscriptions have a limited lifetime and can be terminated by either the push service or the user agent at any time, so both sides must be prepared to manage changes in the subscription state.

The protocol uses HTTP resources and link relations. Six resources are defined: the push service resource, which is used to create subscriptions and whose URL is configured into user agents; the push message subscription resource, which provides read and delete access for a subscription and is identified by the link relation urn:ietf:params:push:set being used for the set and urn:ietf:params:push for the push resource; the push message subscription set resource, which provides read and delete access for a collection of subscriptions; the push resource, used to request delivery of a message and identified by the relation urn:ietf:params:push; the push message resource, which identifies a message accepted for delivery and is deleted by the user agent to acknowledge receipt; and the receipt subscription resource, used to receive delivery confirmations and identified by the relation urn:ietf:params:push:receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: Three parties are involved. The device holds a subscription with the push service, and the application server holds a separate identifier, the push resource, which lets it send messages to that subscription. The push service stores the messages and hands them to the device when it can.

sections.title: Subscribing and Sending a Message
sections.content:
A user agent sends a POST request to its configured push service resource to create a new subscription. A 201 Created response indicates that the subscription was created, and a URI for the push message subscription resource MUST be returned in the Location header field. The push service MUST provide a URI for the push resource corresponding to the subscription in a link relation of the type urn:ietf:params:push. An application-specific method is used to distribute that push URI to the application server, and confidentiality protection and application server authentication MUST be used so that the URI is not disclosed to unauthorised recipients.

Collecting several subscriptions into a subscription set can be a significant efficiency improvement for both the push service and the user agent, and the push service MAY provide a URI for such a set in a link relation of the type urn:ietf:params:push:set. A user agent SHOULD include that set in later subscription requests, and the push service SHOULD return the same set, although it MAY return a new one if it cannot reuse it. A push service MUST return 400 Bad Request for a request with an invalid subscription set, and MAY return 429 Too Many Requests to reject a request that omits one.

An application server requests the delivery of a push message by sending an HTTP POST request to the push resource it was given, with the content of the message in the body of the request. A 201 Created response means the message was accepted, and a URI for the push message resource MUST be returned in the Location header field. That acceptance does not mean the message reached the user agent.
sections.plainLanguage: The device asks the push service for a subscription and gets back two addresses: one it keeps, and one it passes to the application server. The application server posts its message to that second address. The push service replies that it has accepted the message, which is not the same as saying the device has received it.

sections.title: Time-To-Live, Urgency and Topic
sections.content:
A push service can improve the reliability of delivery by storing messages for a period, because user agents are often only intermittently connected. Delaying delivery might also be used to batch communication with the user agent, which conserves radio resources. Some messages are not useful once a certain period has elapsed, so an application server MUST include the TTL header field in its request, with a value in seconds suggesting how long the message should be retained. A push service MUST return 400 Bad Request to a request that omits it, and MAY retain the message for less than requested, indicating this by returning a TTL header field with the actual value, which MUST be less than or equal to the value the application server provided. Once the TTL period elapses the push service MUST NOT attempt delivery. A message with a zero TTL is delivered immediately if the user agent is available, and expires without delivery if it is not.

Urgency exists because a battery-powered device benefits from staying dormant. An application server MAY include an Urgency header field, which indicates the message urgency, and the push service MUST NOT forward that header to the user agent. A message without the header defaults to normal. A user agent MAY include the header when monitoring to indicate the lowest urgency it is willing to receive, and the push service MUST NOT deliver messages of lower urgency. The four values, in order of increasing urgency, are very-low, low, normal and high.

A stored push message can be replaced with new content, which avoids sending outdated or redundant messages when the user agent was offline. Only messages assigned a topic can be replaced: a message with a topic replaces any outstanding message with an identical topic. A topic is a string in a Topic header field, used to correlate messages sent to the same subscription and conveying no other semantics. The field MUST be restricted to no more than 32 characters from the URL and filename-safe Base 64 alphabet, and a push service that receives a request with a Topic field that does not meet those constraints MUST return 400 Bad Request. The Topic value MUST NOT be forwarded to user agents, and it is neither encrypted nor authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: Three header fields tune the delivery. TTL says how long the push service should keep the message. Urgency says how important it is, so that a device sitting on Wi-Fi can be left alone for trivial messages but is woken for urgent ones. Topic lets a new message replace an older one with the same topic, so the device does not receive a queue of stale updates.

sections.title: Receiving Messages and Acknowledging Them
sections.content:
A user agent requests the delivery of new push messages by making a GET request to a push message subscription resource. The push service does not respond to that request; instead it uses HTTP/2 server push to send the contents of push messages as they are sent by application servers. The push service permits the request to remain outstanding, and when an application server sends a message, a server push is generated in association with the initial request. Each push message is pushed as the response to a synthesized GET request sent in a PUSH_PROMISE, made to the push message resource that the push service created when the application server requested delivery. The response headers SHOULD provide a URI for the push resource in a link relation of the type urn:ietf:params:push, and the response body is the entity body from the most recent request sent to the push resource by the application server.

A user agent can also ask for the contents of the subscription resource immediately by including a Prefer header field with a wait preference of 0, in which case the push service MUST generate a server push for all the messages that have not yet been delivered. A 204 No Content status code with no associated server pushes indicates that no messages are presently available, which could be because messages have expired.

To ensure that a message is properly delivered at least once, the user agent MUST acknowledge receipt by performing an HTTP DELETE on the push message resource. If the service receives the acknowledgement and the application requested a delivery receipt, it MUST return 204 No Content to the application server monitoring the receipt subscription. If the service does not receive the acknowledgement within a reasonable time, the message is considered not yet delivered and the service SHOULD continue to retry delivery until its advertised expiration.
sections.plainLanguage: The device leaves a GET request open on its subscription. When a message arrives, the push service answers that same request with a second, pushed response carrying the message body, so the device does not have to poll. When it has processed the message, the device deletes the message resource, which is the acknowledgement, and that is what triggers a delivery receipt back to the application server.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
A push service is likely to have to maintain a very large number of open TCP connections, and effective management of those connections can depend on being able to move them between server instances. A user agent MUST support the 307 Temporary Redirect status code, which a push service can use to redistribute load when a new subscription is requested. A server wishing to redistribute load can use HTTP alternative services, which allows redistribution while keeping the same URIs for resources, and a user agent can ensure a graceful transition by using the GOAWAY frame once it has established a replacement connection.

Storage of push messages based on the TTL header field can be a significant amount of storage, and a service is not obliged to store messages indefinitely. A user agent that does not actively monitor for push messages will not receive messages that expire during that interval, and messages that are stored and not delivered are delivered when the user agent recommences monitoring. To limit the size of messages, the push service MAY return 413 Payload Too Large, but it MUST NOT return that status for an entity body of 4096 bytes or less. A push service MAY expire a subscription at any time, and outstanding requests to an expired resource MUST be answered with 404 Not Found. A user agent removes its subscription by sending a DELETE request to the corresponding URI, and an application server removes a receipt subscription the same way.

The RFC also notes the effect on application reliability. A push service that does not support reliable delivery over intermittent connections or failing applications forces the device to acknowledge receipt directly to the application server, which costs additional power. Reliability matters when messages carry information critical to the state of an application, because repairing the state can be expensive and knowing that a message arrived avoids retransmissions, polling and state resynchronization. It does not matter for messages that are transient, such as an incoming call, or quickly superseded, such as the number of unread emails.
sections.plainLanguage: A push service ends up holding very many open connections and a store of undelivered messages, so the RFC says how to spread the load, when to throw messages away, and how long a subscription lasts. It also argues that delivery receipts matter: without them, applications build their own fallback channels and lose the benefit of push altogether.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol MUST use HTTP over TLS, including any communications between the user agent and the push service and between the application server and the push service, so all URIs use the https scheme. This gives confidentiality and integrity protection for subscriptions and push messages from external parties, but it does not protect the content from the push service itself, which can inspect and modify the message content. Applications using this protocol MUST therefore use mechanisms that provide end-to-end confidentiality, integrity and data origin authentication. The W3C Push API has adopted Message Encryption for WebPush to secure the content of messages from the push service.

The Topic header field exposes information that allows more granular correlation of push messages on the same subject, which might aid traffic analysis by the push service.

On privacy, push message confidentiality does not protect the identity of who is communicating or when. The URIs provided for push resources MUST NOT provide any basis to correlate communications for a given user agent, and it MUST NOT be possible to correlate any two push resource URIs based solely on their contents. The URIs the push service provides to identify a push message MUST NOT allow correlation across subscriptions. User and device information MUST NOT be exposed through a push or push message URI, and a user agent MUST be able to create new subscriptions with new identifiers at any time.

This protocol does not define how a push service establishes whether a user agent may create a subscription. Authorization is managed using capability URLs for the subscription, push and receipt subscription resources. A capability URL grants access to a resource based solely on knowledge of the URL, and it acts as a bearer token: knowledge of a push URI implies authorization to send messages, and knowledge of a subscription URI implies authorization to receive messages or delete the subscription. Encoding a large amount of random entropy, at least 120 bits, in the path component makes a valid capability URL hard to guess.

Push messages that are not successfully authenticated by the user agent will not be delivered, but even a small volume of push messages can exhaust the power reserves of a battery-powered device. Push services SHOULD limit the rate at which messages are sent to individual user agents, MAY return 429 Too Many Requests when an application server exceeds its rate limit, and should include a Retry-After header. Server request logs can reveal subscription-related URIs, so limits on log retention and strong access control are needed to keep them from unauthorised eyes.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS protects the traffic, but the push service sits in the middle and would otherwise be able to read every message, so the application encrypts the payload itself. The identifiers handed out are like keys: whoever holds one can act, so they carry at least 120 bits of randomness and must not reveal who is talking to whom. And the push service should not let anyone flood a device with wake-ups.

messages.label: SUBSCRIBE
messages.note: POST to the push service resource to create a subscription.

messages.label: SUBSCRIPTION CREATED
messages.note: 201 Created, with the subscription URI in Location and the push URI in a Link header.

messages.label: PUSH URI
messages.note: The push URI is handed over over a protected channel.

messages.label: PUSH MESSAGE
messages.note: POST to the push resource, with the message body and a TTL header.

messages.label: PUSH MESSAGE
messages.note: Delivered as a server push on the outstanding request.

messages.label: ACKNOWLEDGE
messages.note: DELETE on the push message resource. A receipt is then sent to the application server.

items.label: Very low
items.desc: The device is on power and on Wi-Fi. The RFC's example is advertisements.

items.label: Low
items.desc: The device is on either power or Wi-Fi. The RFC's example is topic updates.

items.label: Normal
items.desc: The device is on neither power nor Wi-Fi. The RFC's example is a chat or calendar message. This is the default when the header is absent.

items.label: High
items.desc: The battery is low. The RFC's example is an incoming phone call or a time-sensitive alert.

viz.caption: WHAT THE RFC REQUIRES FOR SAFETY

items.title: End-to-end encryption
items.text: TLS protects the connection, but the application must encrypt the message itself, because the push service sits in the middle.

items.title: Hard-to-guess URIs
items.text: A push resource URI acts as a bearer token, so it must carry at least 120 bits of randomness in its path.

items.title: No correlation
items.text: Two push resource URIs must not be correlatable from their contents alone, and no user or device information may appear in them.

items.title: Rate limiting
items.text: The push service should limit how many messages it sends to a single user agent, because a flood of wake-ups can drain a battery.
